newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW -Pfizer gives priority to R&D, marketing.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -Pfizer gives priority to R&D, marketing.

text.p: Pfizer Inc is willing to endure slower earnings growth in the second half as it plows more money into research and marketing, its chief financial officer, David Shedlarz, said Friday.
Pfizer shares fell earlier Friday after Executive Vice President Henry McKinnell acknowledged at a meeting with analysts that second-half earnings growth was likely to be in the single digits.
The stock was off 2-9/16 to 59-3/16 by early afternoon.

Shedlarz reaffirmed he expected 1997 earnings growth of at least 10 percent, noting earnings per share rose 13 percent in recent second quarter and increased 14 percent for the first half of the year over the same periods in 1996.
"So obviously, if you do the math and you choose to pick 10 percent for 1997 earnings growth, the number has to be single digits in the second half of the year to get yourself there," he said.
He said earnings for the rest of 1997 would be affected most adversely by research and development expenses and by "sales and marketing support for existing and new products."

"If growth is tempered in the second half of the year, it will be on the basis of those investments," he said, with research the biggest item as the company ramps up its 1997 R&D spending to $2 billion from $1.7 billion last year.
Research and development expenses in the second half would have to be boosted 20 percent above the 1996 period in order to build Pfizer's ambitious pipeline of new prescription drugs, he said.
It plans to launch three in 1998, including two drugs awaiting approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration: quinolone antibiotic Trovan and Zeldox for schizophrenia.
And Pfizer said it would file a new drug application with the FDA in the current quarter for Viagra, an oral therapy for male erectile dysfunction which it plans to launch next year.

The company announced in April it would build another one million square feet of laboratory space to usher in a later wave of products, increasing Pfizer's stature as a research and development leader intent on boisterous growth.
Shedlarz stressed Friday that Pfizer's second-half 1997 earnings projection was not carved in stone, adding expenses and other factors would tell the tale.
"But we're saying if full-year prospects are at least
10 percent, that gives you a range."
